claim: Positive (male-to-female exposure) engram cells upregulated genes linked to anti-inflammatory responses.
source: Sequencing memory engrams in mice revealed that positive (male-to-female exposure) and negative (foot shock) cells upregulated genes linked to anti- and pro-inflammatory responses, respectively.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1, demonstrating enrichment of anti-inflammatory gene sets in positive engram cells.

claim: Negative (foot shock) engram cells upregulated genes linked to pro-inflammatory responses.
source: Sequencing memory engrams in mice revealed that positive (male-to-female exposure) and negative (foot shock) cells upregulated genes linked to anti- and pro-inflammatory responses, respectively.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1, demonstrating enrichment of pro-inflammatory gene sets in negative engram cells.

claim: Negative engram activation increased anxiety behaviors in 6-month-old mice.
source: Negative engram activation increased anxiety behaviors in both 6- and 14-month-old mice, reduced spatial working memory in older mice, impaired fear extinction in younger mice, and heightened fear generalization in both age groups.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from open field and zero maze tests showing decreased time in center/open areas in 6-month-old hM3Dq mice compared to controls (Figure 3).

claim: Negative engram activation increased anxiety behaviors in 14-month-old mice.
source: Negative engram activation increased anxiety behaviors in both 6- and 14-month-old mice, reduced spatial working memory in older mice, impaired fear extinction in younger mice, and heightened fear generalization in both age groups.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from open field and zero maze tests showing decreased time in center/open areas in 14-month-old hM3Dq mice compared to controls (Figure 3).

claim: Negative engram activation reduced spatial working memory in older (14-month-old) mice.
source: Negative engram activation increased anxiety behaviors in both 6- and 14-month-old mice, reduced spatial working memory in older mice, impaired fear extinction in younger mice, and heightened fear generalization in both age groups.
evidence: Supported by y-maze data showing lower percentage of spontaneous alternations in 14-month-old hM3Dq mice compared to controls (Figure 3c).

claim: Negative engram activation impaired fear extinction in younger (6-month-old) mice.
source: Negative engram activation increased anxiety behaviors in both 6- and 14-month-old mice, reduced spatial working memory in older mice, impaired fear extinction in younger mice, and heightened fear generalization in both age groups.
evidence: Supported by extinction data showing a trend toward increased freezing in 6-month-old hM3Dq mice during extinction (Figure 4c).

claim: Negative engram activation heightened fear generalization in 6-month-old mice.
source: Negative engram activation increased anxiety behaviors in both 6- and 14-month-old mice, reduced spatial working memory in older mice, impaired fear extinction in younger mice, and heightened fear generalization in both age groups.
evidence: Supported by context B generalization data showing increased freezing in 6-month-old hM3Dq mice in a neutral context (Figure 4d).

claim: Negative engram activation heightened fear generalization in 14-month-old mice.
source: Negative engram activation increased anxiety behaviors in both 6- and 14-month-old mice, reduced spatial working memory in older mice, impaired fear extinction in younger mice, and heightened fear generalization in both age groups.
evidence: Supported by context B generalization data showing increased freezing in 14-month-old hM3Dq mice in a neutral context (Figure 4d).

claim: Chronic negative engram activation induced changes in microglial structure in the hippocampus.
source: Immunohistochemistry revealed changes in microglial and astrocytic structure and number in the hippocampus.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing increased ramification index, cell territory volume, and branch lengths in Iba1+ microglia (Figure 5).

claim: Chronic negative engram activation induced changes in microglial number in the hippocampus.
source: Immunohistochemistry revealed changes in microglial and astrocytic structure and number in the hippocampus.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing increased number of Iba1+ cells in 14-month-old hM3Dq mice (Figure 5c).

claim: Chronic negative engram activation induced changes in astrocytic structure in the hippocampus.
source: Immunohistochemistry revealed changes in microglial and astrocytic structure and number in the hippocampus.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing increased branch lengths in GFAP+ astrocytes (Figure 5).

claim: Chronic negative engram activation induced changes in astrocytic number in the hippocampus.
source: Immunohistochemistry revealed changes in microglial and astrocytic structure and number in the hippocampus.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing increased number of GFAP+ cells in both 6- and 14-month-old hM3Dq mice (Figure 5m).

claim: Repeated activation of negative memories induces lasting cellular and behavioral abnormalities in mice.
source: In summary, repeated activation of negative memories induces lasting cellular and behavioral abnormalities in mice, offering insights into the negative effects of chronic negative thinking-like behaviors on human health.
evidence: Supported by the combined behavioral and cellular data showing persistent changes after 3 months of chronic negative engram activation.

claim: Chronic stress is a risk factor for major depressive disorder (MDD).
source: In particular, chronic stress is recognized as a potent risk factor for numerous neuropsychiatric disorders, including major depressive disorder (MDD), generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about the relationship between chronic stress and psychiatric disorders.

claim: Chronic stress is a risk factor for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD).
source: In particular, chronic stress is recognized as a potent risk factor for numerous neuropsychiatric disorders, including major depressive disorder (MDD), generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about the relationship between chronic stress and psychiatric disorders.

claim: Chronic stress is a risk factor for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
source: In particular, chronic stress is recognized as a potent risk factor for numerous neuropsychiatric disorders, including major depressive disorder (MDD), generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about the relationship between chronic stress and psychiatric disorders.

claim: Repeated negative thinking in humans can parallel the effects of chronic stress.
source: In humans, repeated negative thinking can parallel the effects of chronic stress.
evidence: Based on established understanding of psychological processes and their physiological effects.

claim: Repeated negative thinking effects include hippocampal hyperactivity.
source: These effects include hippocampal hyperactivity and accelerating the onset of mild cognitive impairment and dementias (Marchant et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marchant et al., 2020.

claim: Repeated negative thinking accelerates the onset of mild cognitive impairment and dementias.
source: These effects include hippocampal hyperactivity and accelerating the onset of mild cognitive impairment and dementias (Marchant et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marchant et al., 2020.

claim: Reactivating ensembles of hippocampal neurons encoding a positive memory induces anti-depressant effects in mice.
source: For example, our lab previously demonstrated that reactivating ensembles of hippocampal neurons encoding a positive memory is sufficient to induce anti-depressant effects in mice (Ramirez et al., 2015), and studies in rodents have shown that repeated reactivation of negative memories enhances fear responses (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramirez et al., 2015.

claim: Repeated reactivation of negative memories enhances fear responses in rodents.
source: For example, our lab previously demonstrated that reactivating ensembles of hippocampal neurons encoding a positive memory is sufficient to induce anti-depressant effects in mice (Ramirez et al., 2015), and studies in rodents have shown that repeated reactivation of negative memories enhances fear responses (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019.

claim: The ventral hippocampus (vHPC), specifically vCA1, has been extensively studied for its role in emotional processing.
source: The ventral hippocampus (vHPC), specifically vCA1, has been extensively studied for its role in emotional processing.
evidence: Based on established neuroscience literature on hippocampal function.

claim: vCA1 dysfunction is associated with pathological affective states.
source: As a modulator of stress responses, vCA1 dysfunction is intimately associated with pathological affective states (Fanselow and Dong, 2010), and its structure and function are heavily impacted by stressors.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fanselow and Dong, 2010.

claim: vCA1 structure and function are heavily impacted by stressors.
source: As a modulator of stress responses, vCA1 dysfunction is intimately associated with pathological affective states (Fanselow and Dong, 2010), and its structure and function are heavily impacted by stressors.
evidence: Based on established neuroscience knowledge about stress effects on the hippocampus.

claim: vCA1 neurons project to the basolateral amygdala, nucleus accumbens, and prefrontal cortex.
source: Additionally, vCA1 neurons project to various downstream targets and route target-specific streams of information to the basolateral amygdala, nucleus accumbens, and prefrontal cortex.
evidence: Based on established neuroanatomical knowledge of hippocampal connectivity.

claim: vCA1 connections to downstream targets are integral to the formation of emotional memory.
source: These diverse connections are integral to the formation of emotional memory, as well as regulating anxiety and the stress response.
evidence: Based on established neuroscience understanding of hippocampal circuits.

claim: vCA1 connections to downstream targets regulate anxiety and the stress response.
source: These diverse connections are integral to the formation of emotional memory, as well as regulating anxiety and the stress response.
evidence: Based on established neuroscience understanding of hippocampal circuits.

claim: Stimulation of negative engram cells in vCA1 modulates social avoidance behavior.
source: Within vCA1, stimulation of negative engram cells has been shown to modulate social avoidance behavior and enhance fear responses, but whether chronic stimulation of fearful memories produces enduring effects on brain activity and behavior remains unknown (Chen et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2019 and Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Stimulation of negative engram cells in vCA1 enhances fear responses.
source: Within vCA1, stimulation of negative engram cells has been shown to modulate social avoidance behavior and enhance fear responses, but whether chronic stimulation of fearful memories produces enduring effects on brain activity and behavior remains unknown (Chen et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2019 and Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Adverse childhood experiences are a risk factor for the development of psychopathologies later in life.
source: Epidemiological population-based studies in humans have established adverse childhood experiences as a risk factor for the development of psychopathologies later in life.
evidence: Based on established epidemiological findings.

claim: The development of depression and PTSD may increase with the number of adverse childhood events.
source: Notably, the development of depression and PTSD may increase with the number of these adverse events, suggesting an increased susceptibility of the developing, young brain to the perturbations induced by such events (McLaughlin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to McLaughlin et al., 2010.

claim: Aged rodents have increased stress vulnerability compared to younger animals.
source: Aged rodents have increased stress vulnerability, as repeated stress increased anxiety-like behaviors, induced spatial memory impairments, and raised corticosterone levels more compared to younger animals (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: Repeated stress in aged rodents increases anxiety-like behaviors more than in younger animals.
source: Aged rodents have increased stress vulnerability, as repeated stress increased anxiety-like behaviors, induced spatial memory impairments, and raised corticosterone levels more compared to younger animals (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: Repeated stress in aged rodents induces spatial memory impairments more than in younger animals.
source: Aged rodents have increased stress vulnerability, as repeated stress increased anxiety-like behaviors, induced spatial memory impairments, and raised corticosterone levels more compared to younger animals (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: Repeated stress in aged rodents raises corticosterone levels more than in younger animals.
source: Aged rodents have increased stress vulnerability, as repeated stress increased anxiety-like behaviors, induced spatial memory impairments, and raised corticosterone levels more compared to younger animals (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: The anti-inflammatory gene set was enriched in positive engram cells compared to negative engram cells.
source: The GSEA showed that the anti-inflammatory gene set was enriched in positive engram cells, with higher expression compared to negative engram cells (Figure 1c and d).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1c and d.

claim: The pro-inflammatory gene set was enriched in negative engram cells compared to positive engram cells.
source: Further, the pro-inflammatory gene set was enriched in negative engram cells, with higher expression compared to positive engram cells (Figure 1e and f).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1e and f.

claim: The pro-inflammatory gene set in negative engram cells included Spp1, Ttr, and C1qb1.
source: Interestingly, this gene set included Spp1, Ttr, and C1qb1, which are involved in inflammatory processes and oxidative stress.
evidence: Based on the GSEA analysis and known functions of these genes.

claim: Spp1, Ttr, and C1qb1 are involved in inflammatory processes and oxidative stress.
source: Interestingly, this gene set included Spp1, Ttr, and C1qb1, which are involved in inflammatory processes and oxidative stress.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of gene function.

claim: The weights of both young and old mice increased independently of hM3Dq activation across 3 months of stimulation.
source: The weights of both the young and old mice increased independently of hM3Dq activation across the 3 months of stimulation, suggesting normal weight gain with aging (two-way repeated measures [RM] ANOVA; [6 months] interaction: F(2, 34) = 0.2633, p=0.7701; month: F(2, 34) = 14.84, p<0.0001; group: F(1,17) = 1.361, p=0.2594; subject: F(17,34) = 15.44, p<0.0001. Sidak's [month]: 1 vs. 2, p=0.0279; 1 vs. 3, p<0.0001; 2 vs. 3, p=0.0323. [14 months] Interaction: F(2,52) = 2.607, p=0.0833; month: F(2,52) = 7.854, p=0.0010; group: F(1,26) = 0.1275, p=0.7239; subject: F(26,52) = 20.74, p<0.0001. Sidak's [month]: 1 vs. 2, p=0.6942; 1 vs. 3, p=0.0011; 2 vs. 3, p=0.0198) (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of body weight measurements shown in Figure 2c.

claim: There were no decreases in the number of NeuN+ cells in the subiculum, dentate gyrus, and CA1 of the vHPC due to chronic activation.
source: Importantly, there were no decreases in the number of NeuN+ cells in the subiculum, dentate gyrus, and CA1 of the vHPC due to chronic activation, suggesting that we are not inducing a reduction in neuronal cell health with this constant stimulation, as measured by this method (two-way ANOVA; [subiculum] interaction: F(1, 8) = 0.2516, p=0.6295; age: F(1, 8) = 7.341, p=0.0267; group: F(1,8) = 0.00721, p=0.9344. Tukey's [group]: 6MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.9904; 14MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.9744; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and b. [vDG] Interaction: F(1,8) = 0.6806, p=0.4333; age: F(1,8) = 4.423, p=0.0686; group: F(1,8) = 0.0524, p=0.8246; Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d. [vCA1] Interaction: F(1,8) = 2.824, p=0.1314; age: F(1,8) = 0.5443, p=0.4817; group: F(1,8) = 2.947, p=0.1244) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e and f).
evidence: Supported by NeuN immunohistochemistry and cell counting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 6-month-old and 14-month-old hM3Dq mice spent less time in the center of the open field compared to age-matched mCherry mice.
source: In the open field (Figure 3a), 6- and 14-month-old hM3Dq mice spent less time in the center compared to age-matched mCherry mice (two-way ANOVA); interaction: F(1,33) = 0.1438, p=0.7070; age: F(1,33) = 0.5858, p=0.4495; group: F(1,33) = 29.56, p<0.0001; Tukey's multiple comparisons [group]: 6MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.0049; 14MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.0016) (Figure 3aii).
evidence: Supported by open field behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: There were no significant differences in total distance traveled in the open field across all groups.
source: We observed no significant differences in total distance traveled across all groups (two-way ANOVA; interaction: F(1,37) = 0.0016, p=0.9675; age: F(1,37) = 0.6862, p=0.4128; group: F(1,37) = 0.3522, p=0.5565) (Figure 3ai).
evidence: Supported by open field behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: 6-month-old hM3Dq mice had an increase in average speed in the open field compared to mCherry mice.
source: Further, 6-month-old hM3Dq mice had an increase in average speed in the open field compared to mCherry mice (two-way ANOVA; interaction: F(1,38) = 4.003, p=0.526; age: F(1,38) = 0.2346, p=0.6306; group: F(1,38) = 7.306, p=0.0102; (Tukey's [group]: 6MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.0150; 14MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.9532) (Figure 3aiv).
evidence: Supported by open field behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: There were no differences in the number of center entries in the open field across all groups.
source: However, there were no differences in the number of center entries across all groups, indicating that mice in mCherry and hM3Dq groups are entering the center the same number of times, but spending less time per visit (two-way ANOVA; interaction: F(1,41) = 1.236, p=0.2728; age: F(1,41) = 0.4424, p=0.5097; group: F(1,41) = 0.3370, p=0.5648) (Figure 3aiii).
evidence: Supported by open field behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: 6-month-old and 14-month-old hM3Dq mice spent less time in the open arms of the zero maze compared to age-matched mCherry mice.
source: In the zero maze (Figure 3b), the 6- and 14-month-old hM3Dq mice spent less time in the center compared to age-matched mCherry mice (two-way ANOVA; interaction: F(1,38) = 0.5633, p=0.4575; age: F(1,38) = 0.1709, p=0.6816; group: F(1,38) = 40.22, p<0.0001; Tukey's [group]: 6MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.0002; 14MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.0007) (Figure 3bii).
evidence: Supported by zero maze behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the total distance traveled in the zero maze across all groups.
source: No significant differences were observed in the total distance traveled (Figure 3bi) or number of entries into the open area across all groups (two-way ANOVA; [total distance traveled] interaction: F(1,36) = 1.915, p=0.1749; age: F(1,36) = 0.0093, p=0.9237; group: F(1,36) = 0.6022, p=0.4428. [Open area entries] Interaction: F(1,38) = 1.082, p=0.3049; age: F(1,38) = 0.3839, p=0.5392; group: F(1,38) = 3.286, p=0.0778) (Figure 3biii).
evidence: Supported by zero maze behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the number of entries into the open area of the zero maze across all groups.
source: No significant differences were observed in the total distance traveled (Figure 3bi) or number of entries into the open area across all groups (two-way ANOVA; [total distance traveled] interaction: F(1,36) = 1.915, p=0.1749; age: F(1,36) = 0.0093, p=0.9237; group: F(1,36) = 0.6022, p=0.4428. [Open area entries] Interaction: F(1,38) = 1.082, p=0.3049; age: F(1,38) = 0.3839, p=0.5392; group: F(1,38) = 3.286, p=0.0778) (Figure 3biii).
evidence: Supported by zero maze behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: There was no significant difference in average speed in the zero maze across all groups.
source: We also observed no significant difference in average speed across all groups (two-way ANOVA; interaction: F(1,37) = 0.5118, p=0.4788; age: F(1,37) = 1.659, p=0.2057; group: F(1,37) = 0.7180, p=0.4023) (Figure 3biv).
evidence: Supported by zero maze behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: 14-month-old mCherry mice showed a higher percentage of spontaneous alternations in the y-maze than 14-month-old hM3Dq mice.
source: We observed a higher percentage of spontaneous alterations in 14-month-old mCherry than 14-month-old hM3Dq mice (two-way ANOVA); interaction: F(1,40) = 4.088, p=0.0499; age: F(1,40) = 0.3080, p=0.5820; group: F(1,40) = 7.517, p=0.0091; Tukey's [group]: 14MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.0045 (Figure 3cii).
evidence: Supported by y-maze behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: No significant difference in the percentage of spontaneous alternations in the y-maze was observed between 6-month-old mCherry and hM3Dq mice.
source: However, no significant difference in the percentage of spontaneous alterations was observed between 6-month-old mCherry and hM3Dq mice (Tukey's [group]: 6MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.9634) (Figure 3cii).
evidence: Supported by y-maze behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: There were no significant differences in the total distance traveled in the y-maze across all groups.
source: Additionally, we observed no significant differences in the total distance traveled or total number of entries across all groups (two-way ANOVA; [total distance traveled] interaction: F(1,44) = 0.2668, p=0.6081; age: F(1,44) = 0.5106, p=0.4787; group: F(1,44) = 1.181, p=0.2831; Figure 3ci).
evidence: Supported by y-maze behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: There were no significant differences in the total number of entries in the y-maze across all groups.
source: [Total number of entries] Interaction: F(1,40) = 1.332, p=0.2553; age: F(1,40) = 0.2236, p=0.6389; group: F(1,40) = 0.8247, p=0.3692 (Figure 3ciii).
evidence: Supported by y-maze behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: mCherry and hM3Dq mice in the 3- and 11-month groups displayed no differences in freezing behavior during contextual fear conditioning.
source: During this CFC session, mCherry and hM3Dq mice in the 3- and 11-month groups displayed no differences in freezing behavior, as expected (two-way ANOVA; interaction: F(1,42) = 0.1342, p=0.7150; age: F(1,42) = 12.20, p=0.0011; group: F(1,42) = 2.913, p=0.0953) (Figure 4ai–ii).
evidence: Supported by fear conditioning behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: There was an increase in freezing during remote recall between 6- and 14-month mCherry mice.
source: The only significant difference in remote recall behavior was an increase in freezing between 6- and 14-month mCherry mice (two-way ANOVA; interaction: F(1,41) = 2.531, p=0.1193; age: F(1,41) = 10.08, p=0.0028; group: F(1,41) = 6.406, p=0.0153; Tukey's [age]: 6 vs. 14MO mCherry, p=0.0101; 6 vs. 14MO hM3Dq, p=0.6672. [Group] 6MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.0449; 14MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.8890) (Figure 4bi–ii).
evidence: Supported by remote recall behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: There were no significant differences in freezing during extinction across all groups at 6 and 14 months of age.
source: For the extinction session in the same context, there were no significant differences across all groups at 6 and 14 months of age (Figure 4ci–ii).
evidence: Supported by extinction behavioral data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: There was a strong trend showing an increase in freezing during extinction in 6-month-old hM3Dq mice.
source: However, we observed a strong trend showing an increase in freezing in the 6-month-old hM3Dq mice that was like remote recall (two-way ANOVA; interaction: F(1,41) = 2.618, p=0.1133; age: F(1,41) = 2.335, p=0.1342; group: F(1,41) = 5.763, p=0.0210; Tukey's [group]: 6MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.0590; 14MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.9269) (Figure 4di–ii).
evidence: Supported by extinction behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Mice in the hM3Dq groups at both 6 and 14 months of age displayed increased freezing in a neutral context B compared to mCherry controls.
source: Finally, mice were placed in a neutral, novel context B at this remote time point after chronic activation to test for generalization of fear. In this context B, mice in the hM3Dq groups at both 6 and 14 months of age displayed increased freezing in a neutral context compared to mCherry controls (two-way ANOVA; Iinteraction: F(1,41) = 0.09801, p=0.7558; age: F(1,41) = 2.624, p=0.1129; group: F(1,41) = 26.53, p<0.0001; Tukey's [group]: 6MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.0053; 14MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.0026) (Figure 4g and h).
evidence: Supported by context B generalization behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: 14-month-old mice in the hM3Dq group displayed an increase in Iba1+ cells compared to mCherry controls.
source: For microglia (Figure 5a–j, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), 14-month-old mice in the hM3Dq group displayed an increase in Iba1+ cells, while 6-month-old mice did not (two-way ANOVA; interaction: F(1,8) = 7.615, p=0.0247; age: F(1,8) = 3.259, p=0.1087; group: F(1,8) = 13.42, p=0.0064; Tukey's [group]: 6MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.9906; 14MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.0113. [Age] 6 vs. 14MO mCherry, p=0.9876; 6 vs. 14MO hM3Dq, p=0.0704) (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: 14-month-old hM3Dq mice had microglia with increased ramification index compared to controls.
source: Additionally, these 14-month-old hM3Dq mice had microglia with increased ramification index, cell territory volume, and minimum and maximum branch length, suggesting a distinct change in phenotype with negative memory activation (two-way ANOVA; [ramification index] interaction: F(1,8) = 1.908, p=0.2046; age: F(1,8) = 1.950, p=0.2001; group: F(1,8) = 15.11, p=0.0046. Tukey's [group]: 6MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.3513; 14MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.03242 (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: 14-month-old hM3Dq mice had microglia with increased cell territory volume compared to controls.
source: [Cell territory volume] interaction: F(1,8) = 3.494, p=0.0965; age: F(1,8) = 0.05044, p=0.8279; group: F(1,8) = 16.45, p=0.0037. Tukey's [group]: 6MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.4564; 14MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.0129 (Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: 14-month-old hM3Dq mice had microglia with increased minimum branch length compared to controls.
source: [Min branch length] interaction: F(A1,8) = 8.287, p=0.0206; age: F(1,8) = 9.619, p=0.0146; group: F(1,8) = 7.470, p=0.0257. Tukey's [group]: 6MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.9996; 14MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.0174. [Age]: 6 vs. 14MO mCherry, p=0.9985; 6 vs. 14MO hM3Dq, p=0.0141 (Figure 5i).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: 14-month-old hM3Dq mice had microglia with increased maximum branch length compared to controls.
source: [Max branch length] Interaction: F(1,8) = 4.094, p=0.0777; age: F(1,8) = 1.214, p=0.3026; group: F(1,8) = 8.964, p=0.0172. Tukey's [group]: 6MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.8994; 14MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.0309 (Figure 5j)).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: There were no significant differences in the average centroid distance of Iba1+ cells across groups.
source: However, there were no significant differences in the average centroid distance, number of endpoints, and average branch length for Iba1+ cells (two-way ANOVA; [Avg centroid distance] interaction: F(1,8) = 0.7707, p=0.4056; age: F(1,8) = 1.155, p=0.3138; group: F(1,8) = 5.459, p=0.0477. Tukey's [group]: 6MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.7370; 14MO mCherry vs. hM3Dq, p=0.1838; Figure 5f.
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells.

evidence: Supported by citation to Ramirez et al., 2015.

claim: Chronic activation of a positive engram in healthy, unstressed mice may produce behavioral outcomes similar to chronic environmental enrichment.

claim: Chronic environmental enrichment improves cognitive flexibility and memory.
source: Here, we speculate that chronic activation of a positive engram in healthy, unstressed mice may produce behavioral outcomes similar to those effects seen in chronic environmental enrichment, with improved cognitive flexibility, memory, and even enhanced levels of anti-inflammatory proteins like BDNF (see Bayne, 2018 for review).

evidence: Supported by citation to Bayne, 2018.

claim: Repeated negative memory activation showed content- and context-specific effects in other studies.

claim: 'Inhibitory control' of the prefrontal cortex on the hippocampus keeps rumination symptoms at bay in the healthy brain.

evidence: Based on established neuroscience understanding of prefrontal-hippocampal interactions.

claim: Stress may compromise GABAergic signaling in the hippocampus.

evidence: Supported by citations to Alaiyed et al., 2020, Banasr et al., 2017, and Albrecht et al., 2021.

claim: Elevated hippocampal activity and dysfunction of GABAergic interneurons is evident in human patients with major depression and PTSD.

evidence: Supported by citations to Osuch et al., 2001 and Rayner et al., 2016.

claim: Hippocampal activity levels are correlated with behavioral rumination and flashback intensity in patients with major depression and PTSD.
source: This elevated hippocampal activity and dysfunction of GABAergic interneuron is evident in human patients with major depression and PTSD, and the activity levels are correlated with behavioral rumination and flashback intensity (Osuch et al., 2001; Rayner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Osuch et al., 2001 and Rayner et al., 2016.

claim: Fronto-hippocampal inhibitory control via GABAergic signaling underlies the inability to suppress unwanted thoughts.

evidence: Based on established neuroscience findings from human imaging studies.

claim: GABAergic signaling in the hippocampus has been shown to produce impaired extinction of conditioned fear.
source: Further, GABAergic signaling in the hippocampus has been shown to produce impaired extinction of conditioned fear (Müller et al., 2015) and increased anxiety (Crestani et al., 1999).

claim: GABAergic signaling in the hippocampus has been shown to produce increased anxiety.
source: Further, GABAergic signaling in the hippocampus has been shown to produce impaired extinction of conditioned fear (Müller et al., 2015) and increased anxiety (Crestani et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Crestani et al., 1999.

claim: Allostatic load refers to the 'wear and tear' the body experiences as a result of chronic exposure to stressful events.
source: In the context of our findings, the concept of allostatic load refers to the 'wear and tear' the body experiences as a result of chronic exposure to stressful events.
evidence: Based on established concept in stress physiology.

claim: Repeated cycles of allostasis in response to chronic stressors results in allostatic overload.
source: While the body attempts to produce a physiologically adaptive response through the process of allostasis, it is proposed that repeated cycles of allostasis in response to chronic stressors results in allostatic overload.
evidence: Based on established concept in stress physiology.

claim: Allostatic overload is a state where the cumulative impact of chronic stress has overcome the body's ability to cope, ultimately culminating in disease.
source: In this state, the cumulative impact of chronic stress has overcome the body's ability to cope, ultimately culminating in disease (McEwen and Stellar, 1993; McEwen, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to McEwen and Stellar, 1993 and McEwen, 2004.

claim: Rumination has been shown to increase the risk of alcohol and substance abuse, especially in young individuals.

evidence: Supported by citation to Nolen-Hoeksema and Watkins, 2011.

claim: Rumination after a stressful event is linked to insomnia, poor sleep quality, and pre-sleep intrusive thoughts.

evidence: Supported by citations to Guastella and Moulds, 2007 and Busch et al., 2017.

claim: Rumination after a stressful event is linked to an increase in the risk of heart disease and cardiovascular issues via autonomic dysregulation.
source: Rumination after a stressful event is also linked to insomnia, poor sleep quality, and pre-sleep intrusive thoughts, as well as an increase in the risk of heart disease and cardiovascular issues via autonomic dysregulation (Guastella and Moulds, 2007; Busch et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guastella and Moulds, 2007 and Busch et al., 2017.

claim: Experimental activation of recall-induced populations in the dentate gyrus leads to fear attenuation.

evidence: Supported by citation to Khalaf et al., 2018.

claim: Fear attenuation in dentate gyrus recall-induced populations occurs through updating or unlearning of the original memory trace via engagement of the original traumatic experience.
source: Specifically, this study posits that this fear attenuation occurs in neuronal ensembles through updating or unlearning of the original memory trace via the engagement, rather than suppression, of an original traumatic experience.
evidence: Based on interpretation of findings from Khalaf et al., 2018.

claim: There is high overlap between the encoding and recall ensembles when mice are exposed to the conditioning context.
